Yes, it is necessary. This PR is stacked on top of the in-flight pod tracking PR (#141822), which authored TestScheduleOne_PodUpdateDuringBindingCycle against an older master commit before SchedulingAlgorithm refactor (#141020) merged.

When rebased on current master, that test panics with a nil pointer dereference at algorithm.go:460 because prepareForBindingCycle calls sched.algorithm.assumeAndReserve(...) (and handleBindingCycleError calls unreserveAndForget) on a nil sched.algorithm.

nodeInfoSnapshot was already present in the test's Scheduler struct, but sched.initAlgorithm() was missing to instantiate sched.algorithm. It was added here to keep the test suite passing on the rebase; it will cleanly belong in #141822 once that base PR is updated.

pull_request_title: scheduler: gate queue re-entry behind async status patch completion
original_body:
With async failure handling, ScheduleOne returns before the background goroutine finishes waiting on the status patch and calling sched.requeue(...).

Without ExpectUnschedulable: true, the test immediately advances to the PodGatedInQueue: "preemptor-mid-priority" step, which does an unpolled, immediate check (unschedulablePod(...) == nil) and flakes/fails because the pod has not finished requeueing yet.

Setting ExpectUnschedulable: true causes SchedulePod to poll until the pod actually re-enters the unschedulable pool before continuing. This matches the other preemption steps in this file (and line 1839 later in this same test).
cleaned_text: with async failure handling scheduleone returns before the background goroutine finishes waiting on the status patch and calling sched requeue without expectunschedulable true the test immediately advances to the podgatedinqueue preemptor-mid-priority step which does an unpolled immediate check unschedulablepod nil and flakes fails because the pod has not finished requeueing yet setting expectunschedulable true causes schedulepod to poll until the pod actually re-enters the unschedulable pool before continuing this matches the other preemption steps in this file and line 1839 later in this same test
processed_text: async failure handle scheduleone return background goroutine finish wait status patch call sched requeue without expectunschedulable true test immediately advance podgatedinqueue preemptor-mid-priority step unpolled immediate check unschedulablepod nil flake fail pod finish requeueing yet set expectunschedulable true cause schedulepod poll pod actually re-enter unschedulable pool continue match preemption step file line later test

+func TestTakeByTopologyNUMAPackedForResize(t *testing.T) {
+	logger, _ := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
+	testCases := commonTakeByTopologyTestCasesForResize(t)
+
+	for _, tc := range testCases {
+		t.Run(tc.description, func(t *testing.T) {
+			strategy := CPUSortingStrategyPacked
+			if tc.opts.DistributeCPUsAcrossCores {
+				strategy = CPUSortingStrategySpread
+			}
+
+			result, err := takeByTopologyNUMAPackedForResize(logger, tc.topo, tc.availableCPUs, tc.numCPUs, strategy, tc.opts.PreferAlignByUncoreCacheOption, tc.reusableCPUs, tc.mustKeepCPUs)
+
+			if tc.expErr != "" && err != nil && err.Error() != tc.expErr {
+				t.Errorf("expected error to be [%v] but it was [%v]", tc.expErr, err)
+			}
+			if !result.Equals(tc.expResult) {
+				t.Errorf("expected result [%s] to equal [%s]", result, tc.expResult)
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}

I originally preserved it to keep this change narrowly scoped to the reported issue, which specifically involves link-local nameservers containing a node-specific zone such as `%3` or `%eth0`.

pull_request_title: [KUBELET]: Filter scoped link-local DNS servers
original_body:
If all inherited nameservers are filtered and `pod.Spec.DNSConfig` does not add a replacement, kubelet passes CRI a `DNSConfig` with an empty `Servers` list. This can leave the pod without a usable resolver and requires administrator action to fix the node resolver configuration or provide explicit pod DNS settings.

According to the Kubernetes logging guidelines, conditions that may require administrator action should use `logger.Error`; because there is no underlying error value here, `nil` can be passed.

pull_request_title: [KUBELET]: Filter scoped link-local DNS servers
original_body:
Yeah, the intent here is specifically to filter the scoped IPv6 link-local nameservers inherited from the node when "DNSPolicy" is "Default" and the Pod isn't using the host network namespace. Those addresses can be valid on the node but unreachable from the Pod's network namespace because the IPv6 link-local scope/zone is tied to the node's interface.

The "ParseAddr" error check is mainly defensive. We only remove an entry when we can positively identify it as a scoped IPv6 link-local address. If parsing fails for some unexpected value, we preserve it rather than accidentally dropping a nameserver.

original_body:
goroutinesLimiter is an internal struct in pkg/scheduler/backend/api_dispatcher, so it would have to be exported/moved, and its name/design don't match what we do here:

We are not limiting goroutines: `finishFailureWithRequeue` / `finishFailureWithoutRequeue` already spawn the background goroutine so `scheduleOne` doesn't block; the limiter caps how many status patches can be in flight in apiCacher/apiDispatcher concurrently.

Single caller vs. many concurrent waiters: `goroutinesLimiter` is designed for a single caller (`APIDispatcher.run()`), so its `release()` calls `cond.Broadcast()` [goroutines_limiter.go:73](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1be627ab7e9819ac1d468b48de32142129afb7c2/pkg/scheduler/backend/api_dispatcher/goroutines_limiter.go#L68-L74) Here, many failure goroutines can be parked in acquire() at the same time - `Broadcast()` on every release would wake all of them for a single freed slot, whereas a buffered channel wakes exactly one waiter in FIFO order.

pull_request_title: kubelet: check the pod spec for a startup probe in isContainerStarted
original_body:
Thanks for looking at this.

With the gate on the container ends up not started after a restart regardless of this PR, by two separate paths. Once `AddPod` registers the worker, the existing worker lookup below already reports not started. And the worker is fresh, so its `containerID` is empty on the first `doProbe` and does not match the container the runtime still reports; with the gate on that branch seeds the result with `initialValue`, which is `Unknown` for startup (worker.go:296), and keeps it not started until a probe succeeds. The startup probe then runs again. Neither path depends on this change.

Pod readiness from `generateAPIPodStatus` for a container that survived the restart, written as `first sync after the restart` -> `the sync after that`:

| container at restart | gate | before restart | before this PR | after this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| passed its startup probe | off | Ready | Ready -> Ready | Ready -> Ready |
| passed its startup probe | on | Ready | **Ready** -> NotReady | NotReady -> NotReady |
| still in its startup period | off | NotReady | **Ready -> Ready** | NotReady -> NotReady |
| still in its startup period | on | NotReady | **Ready** -> NotReady | NotReady -> NotReady |

Row 1 is the case you raise, on the default gate, and it is untouched: the `Started` short-circuit returns before the new check, so the container keeps Started and the pod stays Ready.

Row 3 is what this PR is for. The pod stays Ready for good, because `Started` is preserved across syncs and `worker.doProbe` stops probing once it is set, so the startup probe never records a result that could correct it.

Rows 2 and 4 end NotReady either way. What goes away there is the Ready the first sync published before the worker was registered, which is what #135795 reports, where it lasted long enough for a PodDisruptionBudget check to pass and let an eviction through.

So the new check does not cause the re-probe or the NotReady. It stops the first sync after a restart from reporting a container as started while its startup probe has not passed.

Every eviction test in this file uses the same labels: `framework.WithSlow()`, `framework.WithSerial()`, `framework.WithDisruptive()`, and `feature.Eviction`. Just followed the same pattern.

- WithSerial: The test modifies kubelet configuration (eviction thresholds, PodPidsLimit), so it cannot run concurrently with other tests.

- WithDisruptive: It deliberately induces PIDPressure on the node, which can affect other workloads.

If I understand your concern correctly, it's that the event message includes the requested and effective PID values, so each event has a unique message. That would prevent the `EventCorrelator` from aggregating similar events effectively, resulting in a separate event for each pod.

Can address this in a few ways:
- Make the event message static (for example, "Pod PID limit was capped to the node podPidsLimit") so it can be aggregated. The detailed values would still be available in the structured log.
- Remove the event and rely on the structured log instead.
- Keep it as-is since its per-pod activity.

Which approach do you think is most appropriate here, or would you recommend a different solution?

> I really wish it had been called out earlier that this code relies on undocumented behavior. The API never said that the status uses the exact same names as published by the driver.

Small pushback on "undocumented". The `CapacityKey` doc defines the mapping as `consumedCapacity[capacityKey]`, with `dra.example.com/memory` on both sides of the example:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4149d3512d94aebbf6b93e18b0778d10e28571d8/staging/src/k8s.io/api/resource/v1/types.go#L581-L585

That's the same contract dra-driver-cpu relies on, and it's what a new driver author reads today. So I'd treat the doc as part of the fix either way.

> Can we consider this literal usage of a QualifiedName as map key a bug in the driver and change what Kubernetes writes into the map?

Worth noting the driver isn't alone in that assumption. Kubernetes itself does the same literal lookup in two places, both keyed by the slice's spelling of the name:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4149d3512d94aebbf6b93e18b0778d10e28571d8/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/nodeallocatabledynamicresources.go#L219
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4149d3512d94aebbf6b93e18b0778d10e28571d8/pkg/controller/resourcepoolstatusrequest/views.go#L298

And dra-driver-cpu doesn't just miss on it, it fails the pod:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu/blob/083f9fafebb9498371bd08c1879afbc5e381faa3/pkg/driver/dra_hooks.go#L147-L150

So if we go with "change what Kubernetes writes", that's three call sites plus the `CapacityKey` doc that all need to move together, and the driver fix has to ship before 1.38.

original_body:
Happy to take this over, per [the Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0409NGC1TK/p1790005963450609).

I gave the synctest rewrite a go first, but it turns out locking a `sync.Mutex` is explicitly [not durably blocking](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.1/src/testing/synctest/synctest.go#L86-L91), so the bubble never notices the deadlock. Against the unfixed controller the test just sits there until `go test` kills it, which is worse than the 1s timeout we started with.

So I went a different way: the handler [probes `ctrl.mutex.TryLock()`](https://github.com/harche/kubernetes/blob/2560ad7c304b07f2c3fa9be31c5c27f39f14336a/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/resourceslice/resourceslicecontroller_test.go#L1895-L1903) before re-entering `Update`. Nothing else runs concurrently in the test, so if the probe fails, `Update` must still be holding the lock. No goroutines, no timeout, and it fails instantly without the fix.

Full diff against master, original commit untouched and the test change in a second one:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...harche:kubernetes:dra-resourceslice-update-errors

If you'd rather keep the goroutine and just bump the timeout to 5s, that's easy too, though it's still a guess and takes the full 5s to fail when it does. Let me know and I'll open the PR.
